title: Chapter 176 – Han's Wall
html:
[The Valley Wall, Pass of Seven Winds – Head Han]

The first thing Han learns about a siege is that it has a smell, and that the smell does not leave.

It is burnt hair and wet iron and the sweet rot of a thing that should have stayed buried. It lives in her cloak and in the tea and in the folds of her own skin. On the second morning she stops noticing it. On the third she wakes in the Gate tower with her cheek on the map table, thinks for one clear moment that she is at home, and then the horn sounds and the smell comes back all at once, like a hand over her face.

She stands. She pins the bandage on her forehead more tightly. She walks out onto the Wall.

It is forty feet high and two miles long, and it was built eleven hundred years ago to keep out an enemy nobody can name. The Sect has repaired it, and sworn oaths on it, and forgotten it. There are moss and swallows in the lower joints. There are carved wind-faces on seven of the buttresses, one for each of the Winds the Pass is named for, and on the first night she watched a crawler the size of an ox tear the face of the Third Wind off with its jaws.

Seven hundred and twelve, she thinks, as she comes out into the gray light. That is the number I have to say first.

Not the beasts. The beasts are beyond counting. Seven hundred and twelve is the number of her pupils who have been carried off the Wall since dusk of the first day, in blankets, on boards, in the arms of friends. She knows two hundred of the names. She will know the rest by dark, because she is the Head, and a Head learns the names.

"Lu Fei," she says.

"Here, Head."

He is crouched at the parapet in a wrapped gray cloak, fussing with his instrument. He is a lean, anxious man of fifty with ink on his cuffs and a way of holding his shoulders as if expecting a blow. The Weights are laid out beside him on a black cloth: nine bronze discs on silk cords, each stamped with a character, each swaying very slightly in no wind. They are the oldest working array-gauge in the Sect. When Qi pressure falls on a section of the Wall, the matching Weight swings.

"Tell me," she says.

"Sections one through four are steady." He does not look up. "Five and six are fair. Seven is worse than yesterday. Eight is..." The fingers on the cord go still. "Head, eight has been dropping since the middle of the night. It was at sixty. Now it is forty."

"And nine?"

He does not answer.

Han waits, and watches the ninth Weight. It hangs at the end of the cloth, quite motionless. It is not swaying at all. It has swung so far down that it has simply stopped, like a pendulum at the end of its arc.

"Nine is gone," says Lu Fei softly. "It has been gone since the fourth hour. The array there is dead. There is only the stone."

* * *

The Wall is a ring of nine sections, and the Sect holds it with fourteen hundred pupils.

Han has them on the stone in three rotations: one on the parapet, one resting in the courtyards behind, one in the kitchens and infirmaries and rope-sheds, doing the thousand small things a war asks of people who will not be thanked. She has made rules. She has made every Elder, down to the youngest, take a turn on the parapet. She has forbidden anyone to climb down beyond the killing ground, for any reason, for any friend, and on the first night she watched a pupil of nineteen break that rule to haul his brother's body out of the dark. She did not stop him. He did not come back.

Rules have costs. She knows this. It is the second thing a siege teaches.

She walks along the parapet with her staff in the crook of her arm, and the pupils straighten as she passes, hollow-eyed, gray-faced, and some of them smile. It undoes her a little. She had not expected them to smile. She had thought the Sect, at the end of its strength, would look the way she feels: cold, and stretched thin, and bitterly sorry. But they are young. They have the stubborn gaiety of the young who have not yet quite grasped that this may be the last thing they do.

"Head!" A boy of sixteen waves from the third tower. "We killed a big one at dawn! It had six legs!"

"Did it?"

"Yes, Head! Pupil Jun did it, with a spear!"

"I'll commend him tonight," Han says. "Eat something."

She says it every time. It is the only advice she has left.

Pupil Jun, when she finds him, is a red-faced boy of seventeen with a split lip and a spear taller than he is. He kneels, when she comes, so fast that he nearly drops the weapon. She makes him stand. She asks him to describe the beast, and he does, in loving detail, six legs and a bone plate like a table and a smell like a flooded cellar, and she listens to the whole thing with her face grave, nodding in the right places. When he finishes, she takes the white ribbon from her own hair and ties it round the haft of his spear, and he goes the color of a plum.

"Don't get killed," she tells him. "It would ruin the commendation."

"No, Head."

"Eat something."

"Yes, Head."

She moves on quickly, before he can see her eyes.

At the ninth section, she stops.

It is the lowest stretch of the Wall, the oldest, built on a shelf of soft limestone where the Pass narrows to a bottleneck. The buttress here has no wind-face. It has only a plain slab of stone, patched in three places with newer, whiter blocks, and above it the array-markers have gone dark. A line of pupils holds it with spears. They are more than usually quiet. At the foot of the parapet, on the dressed floor, a row of blankets is laid out in the shade, each with a pair of boots at the end.

She counts the boots. Eleven.

Elder Gu is waiting for her, as she knew he would be.

* * *

He is the oldest Elder in the Sect, a stooped, square, bald man of seventy-eight with a beard like a white brush and hands like blocks of wood. He was her teacher's teacher's pupil. He taught her the first eight arrays she ever learned. She called him Uncle until she took the Seat, and he called her Head with a faint air of apology ever since.

"It is the footing," he says without greeting. He points down with his staff. "Limestone. It has been dissolving for a thousand years, and the weight of what is pushing on the other side has found the weak place. I have been listening all night. There is a hollow under the buttress the size of a cellar. Another hour, another two, and the whole section will go."

"Can it be shored?"

"With what?" He says it gently. "The array is dead. I have tried to rewrite it. The stone will not take a mark. The Qi in the foundation has been eaten out, I think by the beasts, though I do not know how. They have a way of finding it."

Han looks along the Wall. The sections on either side, eight and one, are manned. A breach at nine does not stop at nine. It lets the tide into the courtyard behind the Gate tower, and the courtyard holds the infirmary and the kitchens and the two hundred pupils who have nowhere else to sleep.

"How long to the hour of failure?"

"If I had to guess..." He closes his eyes. "Dusk. Perhaps a little later."

"And what would hold it?"

He opens his eyes. They are clear and mild, a very light brown, and she realizes with a small cold shock that he has already decided.

"Uncle," she says.

"A foundation array needs a keystone," says Elder Gu. "Something living, to give it a will to hold. Lu Fei knows the forms. It was done once in the first century, at the Seventh Wind. The stone remembers."

"No."

"I am seventy-eight, Head. I have a bad hip and a worse temper. I have taught your three best arrays masters and I have been a very poor husband to a very good woman, who is dead." The beard twitches. "Let me be useful."

"I am not asking you to be useful. I am asking you to live."

"I know." He smiles. He puts his huge, gentle hand over hers on the staff. "That is why you will be a good Head. You always ask. But you will not stop me."

She wants to shout. She wants to seize him by the front of his robe and haul him back down the Wall like a child. Instead she stands in the thin gray morning, with the smell of the siege in her throat, and says nothing. Because he is right, and she is the Head, and the Head knows exactly what a Wall costs.

"Dusk," she says at last.

"Dusk."

"Then you will have your tea first. With me."

He bows. It is a small bow, an old man's bow. "I would like that very much."

* * *

At noon, a boy runs up from the lower ground, and the boy is white.

"Head!" He falls to one knee before her on the stone. "Head, there is a man! On the road, coming through the ward-line, on foot! The sentries wanted to shoot him, and he said, he said..." His eyes are wide as a hare's. "He said he was the keeper. He's bleeding. He's old. I told them to hold their shafts. I ran. I did not know what to do."

Han is already moving.

She does not remember the stairs. She remembers a long blur of gray cloaks and stone, the rattle of her own breath, and then the lower courtyard, and the broken ground below the Gate, and the smoke, the sweet thick smoke of the pyres.

And a figure on the road.

He is thin. That is the first thing, the dreadful thinness, the cloak hanging off him like laundry on a post. His hair is gray, not the black she remembers. His face has fallen in at the cheeks. He leans on a plain staff and walks with the careful, rocking stride of a man who counts every step because he does not trust the next one. There is blood on his cuffs and blood at the corner of his mouth.

She has known Lin Jian for most of her life. She sat across a table from him when he was a quiet young man and she was a junior Elder, and she watched him become the calmest, most maddening man in the Sect's gift. She has seen him fold a cavern, and she has seen him bluff a Grand Elder to silence with nothing in his hand. She has never once seen him look like a man being sanded away.

Fifteen weeks, he says. Perhaps sixteen.

She hears the words, and she does the sum, and for a moment the whole Wall tilts under her feet.

"I was told," she says, and her voice sounds very strange to her, "that you were coming to save us."

"I am coming to try."

She bows. She does not decide to. She bows the Sect's last bow, the one for its dead, with her hands pressed flat together and her forehead low, because he has walked all that way through a river of beasts on a failing body to stand on this ground, and no Head of the Sect has ever done so much, and she has no better thing to give.

And behind her, one by one, a hundred pupils turn around.

Tell me where the wall is weakest, Jian says. I will start there.

"Section nine," says Han.

* * *

He studies it for a long time without speaking.

They stand together on the broken floor under the ninth buttress: Han, and Jian, and Lu Fei with his Weights, and Elder Gu, who has come down the stairs on his stick to see the man he has been told about. Jian crouches with an effort. He lays one hand flat on the limestone and holds it there, and his face goes quiet and far away, as it does when he is listening to something the rest of them cannot hear.

"There is a void," he says. "Twenty feet by thirty. The stone over it is held up by habit."

"That is Elder Gu's estimate as well," says Han.

"Then the Elder is correct." Jian opens his eyes. He looks up at the old man, and a long look passes between them. "He has told you what he means to do."

"He has."

"And you have agreed."

"I was not given a choice," says Han.

"No." Jian stands. It takes him two attempts. "I suspected not." He turns to Gu and bows, deeply, with both hands pressed together, an Elder's bow, a bow between equals. "Elder. You are a better man than I am, and that is no small thing to say today. Would you allow me to try something first?"

Gu's beard twitches. "If it spares me the trouble, young man, I will allow you anything."

"I cannot promise it will."

"Then you may try."

Jian takes a breath. He closes his eyes. And the air around the ninth buttress folds, softly, like cloth, and then he is not standing there at all.

He is under the wall.

Han sees it in the whole bulk of the limestone: a ripple, a tremor, the distant sound of a man moving in a hollow place. The Weights on Lu Fei's cloth give a single sharp swing. Gu grips her arm. Something is happening in the void, something has seized the foundation from below and pushed, a vast gentle pressure, as of a hand lifting a sagging roof.

Nine seconds. Ten. Twelve.

Jian reappears on the courtyard floor in a heap, on his hands and knees, retching blood onto the stone.

"Healer!" Han is kneeling beside him before she knows it. "Lu Fei, get Bell's pills, they're in his belt, now—"

"No." Jian wipes his mouth. His eyes are gray and hollow and very bright. He looks at her with an expression she has never seen on him: a terrible honest apology. "I could not hold it. I tried to brace it from beneath. A fold can carry me through stone, but it cannot hold the stone up. It only holds me." He gestures weakly at the Weights. "How is it now?"

Lu Fei is staring at the ninth cord.

It is swinging. Slowly, a hand's breadth, to and fro.

"It's..." He swallows. "It's alive. Head. Section nine is alive."

"For how long?"

"A few hours. Two. Three." Lu Fei's voice cracks. "It will not hold through the night."

"I know," says Jian quietly. "I only bought time. I am sorry."

* * *

Lan Wen finds her on the stairs.

She comes up out of the courtyard with her white eyes lowered and her hand on the arm of a young guard, a woman of fifty-odd in a clan captain's cloak, scorched along one sleeve. Behind her, in the shadow of the Gate tower, stand the two hundred Garden guards she marched north, ragged and hollow and very upright. Han has been avoiding this conversation for two days. It is the one in which she will have to say what she cannot promise.

"Head Han." Lan Wen bows, a short sharp bow. "My people are on the south stair. We have held sections one and two since yesterday. We have eleven dead and thirty hurt, and I have come to ask what you need."

"More than you have."

"Yes." The white eyes lift. They do not see Han, as such. They see something else, a pressure, a heat, the faint hum of living bodies, and they pass over her face with an uncanny accuracy. "I felt the ninth section go dark in the night. I have been feeling for the hollow ever since. It is large."

"Elder Gu has a plan."

"He does." Lan Wen's mouth thins. "I felt him, an hour ago, when he went into the stone. Not the array. Him. I know what he intends, Head. I only ask that you let my people stand with him, when he does it."

Han stares at her.

"It is not a thing to be done alone," says Lan Wen quietly. "I have not many kindnesses in me. I have this one. Let the Garden stand at his back."

For a moment Han cannot speak. Then she nods, once. "Thank you."

"Don't." The captain turns away. "I will tell you something, and you may do with it what you wish. The Garden has been angry at the Sect for a long time. We thought you too proud, too slow, too sure of your own hall. I think we were right. But I have stood on this wall for two days with your pupils on either side of me, and I have never once seen them run." She pauses. "I wanted you to know that I saw it."

She goes down the stair, steady on her young guard's arm, and Han stands for a long moment with her hand against the cold stone, and then she goes on.

* * *

They have tea at the third hour after noon, in the shade of the Gate tower, and it is the worst tea Han has ever drunk.

The leaf is old and the water is smoke-flavored. The cups are chipped. Elder Gu has insisted on a proper tray and has somehow found one, bamboo, with a faded painting of a heron on its rim, and he sits on a camp stool with the tray on his knees and pours with great ceremony, in the old style, three rounds. Han watches his hands. They are quite steady. They have always been steady.

"I was not a good husband," says Gu, apropos of nothing. He passes her the cup. "I told you. I was on the Wall for thirty winters and in the lecture hall for forty, and in my own house for perhaps six months in all. She never complained. I used to think that meant she did not mind."

"Uncle."

"She minded. She just did not say." He sips. His eyes are on the heron. "I would like to say to you, as you are the Head and I am an old fool who has never said it, that you have been the best of us. I mean that. Not the strongest. Not the cleverest. The best. You are the only Head in my life who ever wept at a funeral."

"I did not weep at the funeral."

"You wept in the cloister afterward. I saw you." He sets the cup down. "I was proud."

She cannot answer. She holds the chipped cup in both hands and looks at the surface of the tea, and sees her own face there, small and broken and very tired.

From the Wall, a long way off, a horn sounds three notes: Section nine, failing.

Elder Gu rises.

He does it slowly, in stages, as the old do. He brushes the dust off his robe. He settles his cloak. He lifts his stick from the floor and tucks it under his arm, and then he turns to Lin Jian, who has been sitting very still against the tower wall, and says, in his mild unhurried voice, "Young man. You have a way of coming back from things. I would not mind learning it."

Jian looks up. His face is gray. His eyes are not dry.

"It is very simple," he says. "You do not. You only seem to."

"Ah." Gu smiles. "Then I shall be in good company."

He bows once more to Han, to the tower, to the broken court. And then he walks away across the smoking ground toward the ninth section, a stooped old man in a plain robe, with a stick under his arm and his white beard blowing a little in the wind, and he does not look back.

* * *

He gives the array its keystone at dusk.

Han is on the Wall for it. She stands at the parapet above the ninth buttress with her hands on the cold stone and watches him go down to the foundation: down the stair, down through the gap in the floor, into the hollow. She hears his voice. It is a low, even murmur, the old forms of the Seventh Wind, and Lu Fei kneels at the Weights with tears running unchecked down his thin face and speaks the answering lines.

The stone drinks it.

She feels it before she sees it: a deep, warm, indescribably gentle thrum, rising out of the limestone like a held breath let go. The ninth Weight swings. Swings wider. Swings, at last, in a great steady arc, and the dead markers along the parapet flicker, one by one, and light. Pale blue first. Then white. Then the full steady gold of a living array.

On the far side of the wall, the tide stops.

It does not retreat. It simply halts, as if it had run into a mirror, and for a long moment the whole pale mass lies still in the dusk, fifty thousand eyeless faces turned up to the stone. Then, slowly, it begins to flow around.

Section nine holds.

The pupils on the parapet are cheering. It is a ragged, hoarse, half-sobbing sound, and it goes along the Wall like fire. Han does not cheer. She stands with her hands on the parapet and her eyes on the place below the buttress where, in the heart of the stone, a light has just been lit that will burn for a thousand years.

"Head." It is Lu Fei, behind her, hoarse. "Head, shall I record it?"

She thinks about it for a long moment.

"Yes," she says. "Write the name on the buttress. The way we do it for the Winds. Gu, the Eighth. And write what he said, at the end, to the young man. Write it plainly."

"What did he say?"

"He said he'd be in good company."

Before the night is out, she does one more thing. She goes down to the courtyard where the dead of the day are laid in rows, and she walks the length of them with a lamp, slowly, as she has every evening. She does not hurry. She reads the names stitched inside each collar, and when there is no name, she asks the pupils standing near, and when no one knows, she says, aloud, unnamed, and loved, and moves on. It is a small ritual. The Elders think it a waste of time. But it is the one hour of the day when nobody asks her for anything, and when she is only a woman holding a light over people who cannot be helped.

At the end of the last row, she finds a boy of fifteen with his hand curled round a wooden whistle. She kneels. She does not know him. She sits there a long while in the lamplight, and then she tucks the whistle into his sleeve, and straightens his collar, and says quietly, "Thank you for standing."

She stays on the Wall all night, with her staff across her knees and her cloak drawn close, and watches the tide move past the dark place where her teacher's teacher's pupil is keeping the stone alive. She does not weep. She has done that already, in the cloister, and he saw.

At the first light, she counts again.

Seven hundred and twelve, she thinks. Seven hundred and thirteen.

She says the number aloud, once, to the cold gray air, and then she begins to say the names.
